Maps of Italy with sf and ggplot2

R
sf
ggplot2
Data Visualization
Tutorial
Maps
A step-by-step guide to evolving a basic Italy map into an advanced, publication-ready visualization
Author

Joao Luiz D’Andrea

Published

October 14, 2025

Introduction

In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated maps of Italy using the sf (simple features) package and ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic map and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.

Maps are excellent for visualizing spatial data, showing regional patterns, and communicating geographic information effectively.

We’ll use spatial data from the rnaturalearth package and create a choropleth map showing regional statistics across Italy.

Setup

First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)      # For data manipulation
library(sf)             # For spatial data handling
library(rnaturalearth)  # For geographic data
library(rnaturalearthdata) # Additional geographic data
library(ggspatial)      # For scale bars and north arrows
library(scales)         # For formatting

# Get Italy map data at country level
italy_country <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", country = "Italy", returnclass = "sf")

# Get Italy regions (admin level 1)
italy_regions <- ne_states(country = "Italy", returnclass = "sf")

# Create sample data: GDP per capita by region (fictional)
set.seed(42)
regional_data <- tibble(
  region = italy_regions$name,
  gdp_per_capita = round(rnorm(nrow(italy_regions), mean = 32000, sd = 8000)),
  population = round(rnorm(nrow(italy_regions), mean = 3000000, sd = 2000000))
) %>%
  mutate(
    gdp_per_capita = pmax(gdp_per_capita, 20000),  # Minimum value
    population = pmax(population, 500000)           # Minimum value
  )

# Join spatial data with statistics
italy_map_data <- italy_regions %>%
  left_join(regional_data, by = c("name" = "region"))

# Preview the data
head(italy_map_data)

Chart 1: Basic Map of Italy

Let’s start with a simple map showing the outline and regions of Italy.

ggplot(italy_map_data) +
  geom_sf()  # Draw the map

Code Explanation

Line 1: ggplot(italy_map_data) - Initializes the plot with our spatial data

Line 2: geom_sf() - Draws the map using the simple features geometry, automatically handling the spatial coordinates

What we have so far: A functional but basic map of Italy. The regional boundaries are visible but the chart lacks color, labels, context, and visual refinement.

Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement

Now we’ll improve the map by adding a choropleth layer, color scale, labels, and better styling.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

  • Choropleth coloring based on GDP per capita
  • Color scale with meaningful breaks
  • Region boundaries with white lines
  • Improved projection for better appearance
  • Title and legend for context
  • Clean theme removing default elements
  • Scale bar and north arrow for orientation
ggplot(italy_map_data) +
  # Fill regions by GDP per capita
  geom_sf(aes(fill = gdp_per_capita), 
          color = "white", 
          linewidth = 0.3) +
  # Apply color gradient
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#fee5d9", 
                      high = "#a50f15",
                      name = "GDP per Capita\n(EUR)",
                      labels = comma_format()) +
  labs(
    title = "Italy: Regional Economic Performance",
    subtitle = "GDP per capita by region (simulated data)",
    caption = "Data source: Simulated regional statistics"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank()
  )

Code Explanation

Lines 2-4: geom_sf(aes(fill = gdp_per_capita)) - Creates a choropleth map with regions colored by GDP per capita, white boundaries, and thin line width

Lines 6-9: scale_fill_gradient() - Applies a sequential color scale from light orange to dark red, with formatted labels

Lines 10-14: labs() - Adds title, subtitle, and caption for context

Line 15: theme_minimal() - Applies a clean base theme

Lines 16-21: theme() - Removes grid lines and axis elements that are unnecessary for maps

What we have now: A much more informative map with regional color coding showing economic differences. The clean styling and proper legend make it presentation-ready.

Chart 3: Advanced Visualization

Let’s take it to the next level with enhanced styling, city markers, annotations, inset maps, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

  • Custom color palette with better breaks
  • Major city markers showing key locations
  • City labels for important places
  • Enhanced borders with Italy outline
  • Regional labels for largest regions
  • Statistical categories instead of continuous scale
  • North arrow and scale bar for orientation
  • Professional typography and spacing
  • Neighboring countries for context
# Get neighboring countries for context
neighbors <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", 
                         country = c("France", "Switzerland", "Austria", 
                                   "Slovenia", "Croatia"),
                         returnclass = "sf")

# Create GDP categories
italy_map_data <- italy_map_data %>%
  mutate(
    gdp_category = cut(gdp_per_capita,
                      breaks = c(0, 25000, 30000, 35000, 40000, 50000),
                      labels = c("< 25k", "25-30k", "30-35k", "35-40k", "> 40k"),
                      include.lowest = TRUE)
  )

# Major Italian cities (approximate coordinates)
major_cities <- tibble(
  city = c("Rome", "Milan", "Naples", "Turin", "Florence", "Venice", "Bologna"),
  lon = c(12.4964, 9.1900, 14.2681, 7.6869, 11.2558, 12.3155, 11.3426),
  lat = c(41.9028, 45.4642, 40.8518, 45.0703, 43.7696, 45.4408, 44.4949),
  population_millions = c(2.9, 3.1, 3.1, 1.7, 1.0, 0.9, 0.4)
) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)

# Define custom color palette
gdp_colors <- c(
  "< 25k" = "#fee5d9",
  "25-30k" = "#fcae91",
  "30-35k" = "#fb6a4a",
  "35-40k" = "#de2d26",
  "> 40k" = "#a50f15"
)

# Create the main map
ggplot() +
  # Add neighboring countries (in gray)
  geom_sf(data = neighbors, 
          fill = "gray95", 
          color = "gray70",
          linewidth = 0.3) +
  # Add Italy regions with GDP categories
  geom_sf(data = italy_map_data,
          aes(fill = gdp_category),
          color = "white",
          linewidth = 0.5) +
  # Add Italy country outline
  geom_sf(data = italy_country,
          fill = NA,
          color = "gray20",
          linewidth = 1.2) +
  # Add major cities
  geom_sf(data = major_cities,
          aes(size = population_millions),
          shape = 21,
          fill = "yellow",
          color = "gray20",
          stroke = 0.8,
          alpha = 0.8) +
  # Add city labels
  geom_sf_text(data = major_cities,
               aes(label = city),
               size = 3,
               fontface = "bold",
               nudge_y = 0.3,
               color = "gray20") +
  # Apply custom color palette
  scale_fill_manual(values = gdp_colors,
                    name = "GDP per Capita (EUR)",
                    na.value = "gray90") +
  # Size scale for cities
  scale_size_continuous(name = "City Population\n(millions)",
                       range = c(2, 8),
                       breaks = c(1, 2, 3)) +
  # Set coordinate system
  coord_sf(xlim = c(6.5, 18.5), 
           ylim = c(36.5, 47.5),
           expand = FALSE) +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "Italy: Regional Economic Landscape and Major Urban Centers",
    subtitle = "GDP per capita varies significantly from north to south | Major cities marked by population size",
    caption = "Data source: Simulated regional statistics | Map data: Natural Earth | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add north arrow
  annotation_north_arrow(
    location = "tl",
    which_north = "true",
    pad_x = unit(0.2, "in"),
    pad_y = unit(0.3, "in"),
    style = north_arrow_fancy_orienteering
  ) +
  # Add scale bar
  annotation_scale(
    location = "bl",
    width_hint = 0.25,
    pad_x = unit(0.2, "in"),
    pad_y = unit(0.2, "in")
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16,
                              hjust = 0.5,
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "#5A6C7D",
                                  hjust = 0.5,
                                  lineheight = 1.3,
                                  margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D",
                                hjust = 0.5,
                                margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "gray80"),
    legend.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10),
    
    # Panel styling
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "aliceblue", color = NA),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)
  )

Code Explanation

Lines 2-5: Retrieves neighboring countries’ boundaries using ne_countries() for geographic context

Lines 8-14: Creates GDP categories using cut() to convert continuous values into meaningful brackets

Lines 17-25: Creates a tibble of major Italian cities with coordinates and converts to spatial format using st_as_sf()

Lines 28-34: Defines custom color palette for GDP categories, progressing from light to dark

Line 37: ggplot() initializes the plot

Lines 39-42: geom_sf() adds neighboring countries in light gray for context

Lines 44-47: geom_sf() adds Italy regions colored by GDP category with white boundaries

Lines 49-52: geom_sf() adds Italy’s country outline with thick dark border

Lines 54-60: geom_sf() adds major cities as circles sized by population

Lines 62-67: geom_sf_text() adds city name labels above the markers

Lines 69-71: scale_fill_manual() applies custom color palette

Lines 73-75: scale_size_continuous() controls city marker sizes

Lines 77-79: coord_sf() sets the bounding box and removes padding

Lines 81-85: labs() adds comprehensive title, subtitle, and caption

Lines 87-93: annotation_north_arrow() adds a decorative north arrow in top left

Lines 95-100: annotation_scale() adds a scale bar in bottom left

Line 101: theme_void() starts with blank canvas (appropriate for maps)

Lines 102-125: Comprehensive theme customization including: - Centered titles and caption - Legend styling with background box - Light blue panel background (representing water) - Proper margins for professional appearance

Final result: A publication-ready map of Italy that clearly communicates regional economic patterns with major cities marked. The combination of choropleth coloring, city markers, neighboring countries for context, north arrow, and scale bar creates a comprehensive and professional visualization suitable for reports, presentations, or publications.

Comparison: All Three Charts

Here’s a side-by-side view of our progression:

Aspect Basic Intermediate Advanced
Readability Poor (no data, just outlines) Good (choropleth, legend) Excellent (categories + cities + context)
Context None Title & subtitle Full context with neighbors & scale
Visual Appeal Plain outlines Color gradient Custom palette + city markers
Data Layers Borders only Choropleth Choropleth + cities + countries
Geographic Info Regions visible GDP values Categories, population, orientation
Professional Use Not recommended Acceptable for internal use Publication-ready

Key Takeaways

Tip

Tips for Creating Better sf Maps in R:

  1. Use appropriate projections - Consider using st_transform() to convert to appropriate coordinate systems (e.g., EPSG:3857 for web maps)

  2. Choose color scales wisely - Use sequential scales for continuous data, diverging for data with meaningful midpoint, categorical for discrete groups

  3. Add geographic context - Include neighboring regions, bodies of water, or landmarks to help viewers orient themselves

  4. Label strategically - Add labels for major features but avoid cluttering; use geom_sf_text() or geom_sf_label()

  5. Include scale and orientation - Always add north arrow and scale bar for maps showing unfamiliar areas

  6. Mind the aspect ratio - Use coord_sf() with appropriate xlim/ylim to avoid distortion

  7. Layer thoughtfully - Order layers from background to foreground: context → main data → annotations → labels

  8. Use theme_void() for clean maps - Remove axes and grid lines that are unnecessary for geographic visualization

  9. Consider accessibility - Use colorblind-friendly palettes and ensure sufficient contrast

  10. Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("map.png", width = 10, height = 12, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

Next Steps

Try applying these principles to other map visualizations:

  • Point maps showing locations of events or facilities
  • Flow maps showing migration or trade patterns
  • Interactive maps using leaflet or mapview
  • Animated maps showing changes over time with gganimate

Want to create interactive maps?

You can make your maps interactive using leaflet:

library(leaflet)

# Create color palette
pal <- colorNumeric(palette = "YlOrRd", 
                   domain = italy_map_data$gdp_per_capita)

# Create interactive map
leaflet(italy_map_data) %>%
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron) %>%
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~pal(gdp_per_capita),
    fillOpacity = 0.7,
    color = "white",
    weight = 1,
    popup = ~paste0("<strong>", name, "</strong><br>",
                   "GDP per capita: €", 
                   format(gdp_per_capita, big.mark = ","))
  ) %>%
  addLegend(
    pal = pal,
    values = ~gdp_per_capita,
    title = "GDP per Capita",
    position = "bottomright"
  )

This creates an interactive map where users can zoom, pan, and click regions for detailed information.

Alternative: Bubble Map

Here’s a bonus approach showing population as proportional circles:

# Get region centroids for bubble placement
italy_centroids <- italy_map_data %>%
  st_centroid() %>%
  cbind(st_coordinates(.))

ggplot() +
  # Base map with light fill
  geom_sf(data = italy_map_data,
          fill = "gray98",
          color = "gray60",
          linewidth = 0.3) +
  # Add country outline
  geom_sf(data = italy_country,
          fill = NA,
          color = "gray20",
          linewidth = 1) +
  # Add population bubbles
  geom_point(data = italy_centroids,
             aes(x = X, y = Y, size = population, fill = gdp_per_capita),
             shape = 21,
             color = "white",
             stroke = 0.5,
             alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_size_continuous(name = "Population",
                       range = c(2, 20),
                       labels = comma_format()) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#fee5d9",
                     high = "#a50f15",
                     name = "GDP per Capita",
                     labels = comma_format()) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Italy: Regional Population and Economic Output",
    subtitle = "Bubble size represents population, color shows GDP per capita"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 10)),
    legend.position = "right"
  )
